name: Dioxybenzone

lead: Dioxybenzone (benzophenone-8) is a UV filter that absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA, adding coverage that helps protect skin from sun aging. It appears in the US sunscreen monograph.

Its benzophenone core absorbs ultraviolet light and dissipates the energy, the same general mechanism as other benzophenone filters. Very little published research addresses it specifically, so its appearance benefit follows from sunscreens in general.

paras: It is used as one component in a combined filter system in sunscreens. Dedicated information on routines or results for dioxybenzone itself is sparse.

No dioxybenzone-specific human safety data appear in the sources. Studies of benzophenones as a class, mainly oxybenzone, have looked at environmental presence, coral toxicity and cell-level hormone activity.

angle.text: Dioxybenzone (benzophenone-8) is a sunscreen filter in the US monograph that adds UVB and short-UVA coverage, protecting skin from sun-driven aging. It has almost no dedicated research, so its benefit is inferred from sunscreens as a class.

lead: Dioxybenzone, also called benzophenone-8, is a benzophenone-derived sunscreen ingredient that absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA light.[1] Chemically it is (2-hydroxy-4-methoxyphenyl)(2-hydroxyphenyl)methanone, a yellow powder that is insoluble in water.[1]

Wikipedia lists it among sunscreen agents approved by one or more agencies without naming which, and gives no safety or history information.[1] Research on benzophenone UV filters as a class, mainly the better-known benzophenone-3 (oxybenzone), has examined environmental occurrence, hormone-related activity in cells and coral toxicity; dioxybenzone itself is rarely the subject of these studies.[2][3]

paras: Dioxybenzone has a molar mass of about 244 g/mol, is moderately soluble in ethanol and isopropanol, and is a yellow powder at room temperature.[1]

It is used as a sunscreen ingredient to absorb UVB and some UVA radiation.[1] The US sunscreen monograph has listed it among permitted active ingredients, according to the entry's compilation notes.[1]

Benzophenone UV filters as a group have been measured in water, marine organisms and human samples.[2][4] A 2019 study compared four benzophenone filters in coral and a 2018 study examined thyroid-related activity of major benzophenones in cell lines and zebrafish embryos.[3][5] These studies concern the class and primarily its better-known members rather than dioxybenzone specifically.
No studies found. Studies of benzophenone filters in general are environmental or laboratory-based.[2][3][5]
